The chord-to-radius ratio (c/R) ranged from 0.25 to 0.74 in the experiments.
The diameter-based Reynolds numbers tested were between approximately 1.6 × 10^5 and 2.7 × 10^5.
The optimal tip-speed ratio (λ) ranged from 2.3 to 3.6, with the highest values for low c/R and the lowest for high c/R.
Increasing toe-out preset pitch (more negative α_p) resulted in lower performance in the upstream region but higher performance in the downstream region.
Increasing net camber, whether through virtual or geometric camber, led to higher upstream performance but lower downstream performance.
The authors proposed using net camber (γ_net) and net incidence (α_net) as composite variables to better understand turbine performance and design behavior.
The optimal preset pitch angle (α_p) was found to be more negative as c/R increased, in order to reduce the upstream angle-of-attack and delay stall.

The authors found that the optimal performance occurred at a relatively constant net incidence of 0° to +1°, suggesting that virtual incidence is the main driver of optimal preset pitch at a given c/R or camber.
The authors noted that the effects of increasing chord length (c) dominated, causing the chord-based Reynolds number (Re_c) to grow with increasing c/R.

The authors assumed that the simple summation of virtual and geometric factors best represents their combined influence on turbine performance, though they acknowledged this as a significant assumption.
